title: Age-related preference for geometric spatial cues during real-world navigation

findings.consequent: Preference for geometry-based cues in reorientation
findings.statement: Older adults show stronger preference for geometric (geometry-based) cues compared to landmark cues during navigation reorientation in a real ecological environment
findings.quote: a majority of older subjects reoriented and navigated according to the geometry of the environment, apparently neglecting the rotation of the landmarks

stimulus_description.setup: Real ecological environment with obstacle-free street-like maze

findings.mechanism: Perceptual/cognitive deficit in extracting environmental landmarks due to age-related decline in landmark encoding

findings.consequent: Proportion of subjects orienting to geometry across trials
findings.statement: Older adults show significantly higher proportion orienting to geometry across learning trials
findings.quote: there was a significant difference in the proportion of subjects who oriented based on geometry across the two age groups

findings.antecedent: Age group and cue preference (geometry vs landmark)
findings.statement: Reorientation time shows different trajectories for geometry vs landmark groups; older adults using landmarks show longer reorientation times
findings.quote: older adults used landmarks spent significantly longer time reorienting across all learning trials
findings.mechanism: Increased cognitive effort required to process and utilize landmark information in aging

findings.statement: Older adults show significantly slower walking speed during learning phase compared to young adults
findings.quote: older adults showed significantly longer time reorienting across all learning trials
findings.mechanism: Age-related motor decline and cognitive-motor resource allocation

findings.statement: Older adults show significantly larger heading deviations (angular errors) from goal heading during reorientation
findings.quote: heading deviation showed significantly larger values for older subjects
findings.mechanism: Impaired ability to align body direction with goal location

findings.statement: Older adults require significantly longer time to reach goal location during navigation
findings.quote: it required longer for older subjects to reach the goal location (escape latency)
findings.mechanism: Reduced walking speed and increased time in exploration behaviors

findings.antecedent: Cue preference (geometry vs landmark group) and age
findings.statement: Geometry group made fewer exploratory (eye) fixations on wall panels compared to landmark group
findings.quote: geometry group made fewer exploratory fixations compared to the landmark group
findings.mechanism: Reduced exploratory visual behavior in geometry-preferring subjects

findings.consequent: Floor fixations during reorientation vs navigation
findings.statement: Both groups show decrease in floor fixations from reorientation to navigation phase
findings.quote: Ground fixations of the landmark group (n=22) did not differ across the same panels
findings.mechanism: Shift in attention allocation as task progresses from reorientation to goal-directed navigation

findings.statement: Older adults produce significantly more explorative fixations during reorientation compared to navigation phase; pattern differs from young adults
findings.quote: Older adults produced more explorative fixations during the reorientation period
findings.mechanism: Increased reliance on exploratory visual scanning in older adults during spatial learning

findings.antecedent: Oculomotor behavior during learning (eye gaze patterns)
findings.statement: Gaze dynamics and fixation spatio-temporal characteristics during learning predict cue preference in probe phase with 80% accuracy
findings.quote: Performance of a generalized linear model (trained on basis of fixation spatiotemporal characteristics) in predicting spatial cue preference on a single-subject basis suggests that gaze dynamics is indeed predictive of the spatial cue coding used
findings.mechanism: Early visual exploration patterns encode emerging spatial preference

findings.consequent: Visual and cognitive correlates of geometry preference (PCA component 1)
findings.statement: Age groups differ significantly in visual/cognitive profile associated with geometry preference, with older adults showing distinct pattern in perspective-taking ability
findings.quote: older subjects in the geometry group were impaired specifically in the perspective-taking test
findings.mechanism: Age-related changes in visual-cognitive abilities differentially associate with spatial cue preference

findings.antecedent: Age group (young vs older adults) during learning
findings.statement: Young adults show significantly faster learning (steeper decline in reorientation time) across trials compared to older adults
findings.quote: a significant difference in age effects on the reorientation period during learning
findings.mechanism: Age-related slowing of spatial learning and memory consolidation

findings.statement: Older adults show higher fixation counts (more frequent eye fixations) during learning phase
findings.quote: older adults show increased fixations during learning phase
findings.mechanism: Compensatory visual scanning strategy in aging

findings.statement: Landmark group travels significantly longer distance compared to geometry group before reaching goal
findings.quote: landmark group spent more time traversing distance compared to young subjects
findings.mechanism: Less efficient path planning in landmark-based navigation

findings.consequent: No significant effect of cue preference on navigation variables
findings.statement: No significant interaction between age and cue preference in any of the navigation variables analyzed, suggesting cue bias in cue preference in older subjects is independent of age
findings.quote: did not find an interaction between age and cue preference in any of the variables analysed

findings.antecedent: Visual exploration (proportion explorative fixations) during learning
findings.consequent: Cue preference strength in probe phase
findings.statement: Visual exploration patterns during learning show relationship to cue preference development, with age-dependent effects
findings.quote: the proportion of explorative and exploitative fixations during the reorientation period and subsequent navigation periods across learning trials
findings.mechanism: Differential visual exploration strategies affect spatial learning outcomes

findings.consequent: Allocentric strategy deficit in spatial navigation
findings.statement: Advanced age is associated with specific difficulty in using allocentric (landmark-based) navigation strategies and preference for geometric/room-configuration cues
findings.quote: geometry-based coding is mediated by specific oculomotor signatures, independently of age
findings.mechanism: Age-related decline in landmark-encoding ability and reduced capacity to maintain landmark-based allocentric reference frames

findings.antecedent: Capacity to use landmarks efficiently (allocentric ability)
findings.consequent: Dependence on geometry and room-configuration cues in navigation
findings.statement: The observed age-related deficit in landmark use cannot be attributed solely to age-related postural constraints; rather it reflects impaired encoding and utilization of landmark information
findings.quote: capacity to efficiently use landmarks for navigation improves in early development, but deteriorates with aging
findings.mechanism: Cognitive decline in landmark encoding, maintenance, and integration into spatial memory

limitations: Relatively small sample size (N=39, with one older adult excluded due to data error)
Limited to single ecological environment with specific geometric properties
No explicit blinding in data collection or analysis (acknowledged)
Cross-sectional design limits causal inference about aging mechanisms
Relatively narrow age ranges within groups (19-37 years for young, 61-81 years for older)
No control for individual differences in spatial ability outside of measured variables
Limited generalizability to other types of environments (e.g., more complex, outdoor natural settings)

metadata.notes: This paper represents a well-executed empirical study of spatial navigation in aging with careful experimental control and measurement of oculomotor behavior as behavioral signature of spatial strategy. The distinction between geometric and landmark-based cues is theoretically important for understanding allocentric vs egocentric strategy shifts in aging. Multiple findings support the primary claim of age-related geometry preference. Visual/cognitive correlates analysis (PCA) provides mechanistic insight. Study demonstrates that gaze patterns during learning predict subsequent spatial preference (80% accuracy), suggesting this is a robust behavioral phenomenon. The null finding on age-cue interaction is notable: it suggests the geometry preference in older adults emerges from factors independent of age per se, potentially reflecting individual differences in spatial processing capacity or strategy selection.
